guides.title: Egyptian writing, from hieroglyphs to household letters
guides.description: Follow Egyptian writing down the Nile through carved signs, inked letters, school texts and workers’ accounts.
guides.intro: A father lobbies for his son to become a scribe by making a coppersmith’s job sound terrible. A tomb worker’s absence goes into a register in red ink. A tax collector writes a receipt for a pigeon house. Follow such records and the writing systems that carried them along the Nile, then read surviving originals alongside their English translations.
guides.scope: Writing in Egyptian from the late fourth millennium BCE to late antiquity, with examples of Greek and Akkadian in multilingual Egypt and the continuing use of Coptic in worship.

sections.heading: From grave tags to pyramid walls

paragraphs.text: At the cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos, excavators found small perforated labels with incised signs in the late fourth-millennium BCE Tomb U-j. They are among the earliest surviving evidence for Egyptian writing. Some signs resemble later hieroglyphs, but a label offers much less language to work with than a letter. Scholars differ on how fully those early marks encoded speech and what the labels identified.

By the late third millennium BCE, the pyramid of Unas at Saqqara had a burial chamber covered in spells for the deceased king. The surviving Pyramid Texts from Unas are the earliest known examples of that corpus. Their setting shows one purpose of putting words on stone, while the Abydos labels show that portable objects were part of Egyptian written culture from early on.

Hieroglyphs are the familiar picture-shaped signs of temple walls and tombs. A sign might record a consonant or group of consonants, stand for a word, or classify a word written alongside it. A reader could use the picture to recognize a sign while reading the sounds or meaning that the script assigned to it. Hieroglyphs could also be drawn in ink.

Hieratic was the quickly written companion to hieroglyphs. Different hands suited letters, accounts, teaching texts or ritual books. A scribe could brush it onto papyrus or write a short message on a chip of limestone or a broken pot. Later, priests retained hieratic for some religious writing while Demotic became the usual script for many contracts and accounts.

Demotic took shape in the first millennium BCE. It names both a highly cursive script and a later stage of Egyptian. Business and legal records survive in it, along with fiction, ritual and scholarship. Greek was used alongside Egyptian in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. The second-century CE temple library at Tebtunis preserves Greek beside hieroglyphic, hieratic and Demotic texts.

Coptic names the latest stage of the Egyptian language and the alphabet used to write it. That alphabet uses Greek letters plus signs derived from Demotic for Egyptian sounds Greek could not readily represent. Experiments in writing Egyptian with Greek letters predate the widespread use of Coptic in late antiquity. Coptic preserved letters and accounts as well as Christian texts, and it is still used in worship.

sections.heading: Different scripts in the same place

paragraphs.text: Old, Middle and Late Egyptian usually refer to stages of the language. A script is the set of signs used to write it. Middle Egyptian outlived its main period as a spoken form and remained in use for formal and religious texts. A tax receipt and a temple inscription made in the same century could use different scripts and different varieties of Egyptian.

The Amarna archive widens the picture. In the fourteenth century BCE, the Egyptian court received letters from other rulers on clay tablets. Most of these letters used Akkadian written in cuneiform. At the far end of the map and nearly two millennia later, people still incised Egyptian signs at Philae. The latest known dated hieroglyphic graffito there is from 394 CE and the latest dated Demotic graffito from 452 CE. These dates record surviving inscriptions, while the language continued in Coptic.

sections.heading: Household mail, a bull sale and a tax receipt

paragraphs.text: Heqanakht’s family letter reads like a long-distance meeting about the household budget. After a low Nile flood, the priest explains his decision to cut rations and tells the people managing his property how to distribute grain. A different letter from western Thebes directs the recipient to leave Sihathor out of a distribution. The papyrus is damaged, and the identity of the thing being handed out remains uncertain.

Other records put a price on a bull, request a particularly good bird or document a tax on a pigeon house. The bull’s price was reckoned in copper rings, while the transaction included goods such as linen and oil. The pigeon-house receipt names several women together and accounts for a surcharge. Centuries later, letters in Coptic carried an appeal from two women to a hermit, a request for two donkeys and a message instructing a deacon to give lentils to the bearer of the potsherd.

The craftspeople living at Deir el-Medina carved and decorated royal tombs. Their settlement and work sites generated records about shifts, supplies, deliveries, debts and disputes. Offcuts from the building work gave writers an inexpensive surface. The register below is exceptional for its size, with black ink for names and dates and red for the reasons people missed work.

During the reign of Ramesses III, the crew stopped work over late food rations. The scribe Amunnakht documented their actions, including sit-ins at funerary temples and a demand that the officials report their case. An attendance clerk and a strike chronicler can record the same workforce from very different positions.

Some reasons for absence were other work. One man was carrying stones for a scribe. Another visited people and prepared remedies. Entries about illness, a scorpion sting and brewing beer point to the work and obligations that could keep a person away from the tomb. A separate inventory records furniture, cloth and oil, while an annotated map shows the houses of goldworkers near roads, mountains and a temple in the Eastern Desert.

sections.heading: Scribal satire, fiction and love songs

paragraphs.text: The Teaching of Khety stages a father’s argument for sending his son Pepy to writing school. It exaggerates the grime and discomfort of other jobs to make a scribe’s career sound appealing. Surviving copies and extracts show that scribes kept circulating the joke. A familiar-sounding household request can amuse a modern reader, while Khety’s comparisons are deliberately extravagant.

Love songs circulated on papyrus and ostraca. Their speakers can turn the physical landscape into a test of devotion. The poem below makes the Nile crossing both dangerous and possible: the crocodile shrinks in the speaker’s imagination as he presses on.

The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor lets a long adventure and an encounter with a giant serpent end in a sharp exchange between two people who have returned from a mission. In another collection of stories, preserved on the Westcar Papyrus, the young royal storyteller Khafra entertains his father with the tale of a magician who makes a tiny wax crocodile come to life. Tales like these were copied and transmitted alongside much more practical records.

Different kinds of writing survive in different concentrations. At Saqqara an inscription can still be read in its architectural setting. The Met’s Theban archive of Heqanakht was excavated from a burial, with some sheets still folded and sealed. Other records reached modern collections through dealers and have less secure findspots. The Deir el-Medina absence register is attributed to that village from its contents, including the people it names.

The registers and scraps give access to particular literate communities and to people who could ask someone else to write. The distinction matters when a text seems to speak directly: Amunnakht transmits demands voiced by workers, a receipt records several women as taxpayers, and the love poem presents a speaker whose name is unknown. Read each source for who spoke, who took down the words and why the object was kept or discarded.

guides.title: The Rosetta Stone
guides.description: A priestly decree, a multilingual inscription and the route from Rashid to London.
guides.intro: Near the mouth of the Nile in 1799, French troops found a slab that had been reused as building stone. More than two thousand years earlier, Egyptian priests had ordered copies of their decree set up in temples. Three versions survive on the fragment. Comparing them helped scholars recover how hieroglyphs recorded the sounds of Egyptian.
guides.scope: From Ptolemaic Egypt in 196 BCE to nineteenth-century decipherment and the debate over the stone’s custody.

map.scope: A modern regional map shows the decree’s Egyptian setting, the fort locality and transfer, and the stone’s current London collection.

paragraphs.text: The inscription records a decision by a council of priests in 196 BCE at Memphis, where the young Ptolemy V Epiphanes celebrated his coronation. The decree describes royal benefits such as temple support, remission of certain dues and relief for prisoners. In return the priests prescribed new honors for the king, including cult images and recurring observances. It shows priests publicly affirming a dynasty that was dealing with revolts and political strain.

The closing instructions called for copies in temples. Other fragments and versions of the Memphis Decree help scholars compare readings. Memphis marks the council that issued the decree, and Rashid marks where this particular fragment was recovered. The complete route from its original temple setting to the later fort is uncertain.

The upper register is Egyptian in hieroglyphs, the middle is Egyptian in Demotic and the lower register is Ancient Greek. All three communicate the decree, with differences in formulation. The stone is a fragment of a much larger granodiorite stela. The hieroglyphic register has lost much of its text, so the surviving Greek and Demotic carry more of the decree.

cells: The formal script of temple inscriptions. Much of this section is missing.
The contemporary cursive script, rendered here by carving instead of ink.
The version European scholars could already read and use for comparison.

sections.heading: What the stone says about itself

paragraphs.text: The Greek version ends with instructions to write the decree on hard stone in the three scripts visible on the slab. The copies were to stand near images of the king in temples. The decree sets out both the honors the priests had agreed to observe and a way to display that decision in the different registers of Ptolemaic government and ritual.

In 1799, during the French occupation, troops rebuilding a fort near Rashid uncovered the inscribed fragment in reused building material. French officer Pierre-François Bouchard is associated with recognizing the find. The fort is now called Qaitbay Fort and is also known as Fort Julien. The mapped point indicates the vicinity of the fort. Copies of the inscriptions circulated, allowing scholars to work from impressions and drawings far from the original.

Silvestre de Sacy and Johan David Åkerblad used the Greek text to identify names and some sound values in Demotic. Thomas Young developed correspondences between Demotic and hieroglyphic signs and worked out sound values in the hieroglyphic name of Ptolemy. A royal name inside an oval enclosure, called a cartouche, gave scholars a manageable group to align with a name in Greek.

Jean-François Champollion compared names from multiple monuments and drew on his knowledge of Coptic, a later form of Egyptian. Reading older Egyptian royal names as well as Greek and Roman ones helped establish that sound signs were fundamental to the system. His 1822 letter to Bon-Joseph Dacier announced the breakthrough. A wider understanding of how sound signs worked alongside word signs and classifiers grew through further study of Egyptian texts.

British and Ottoman forces defeated the French in 1801. With the capitulation at Alexandria, British officials took possession of the stone. It entered the British Museum in 1802, where it is catalogued as EA24. The military handover, the modern collection and the stone’s possible ancient display site are separate parts of its history.

Egyptian archaeologist and former antiquities minister Zahi Hawass has called for the stone’s return, citing its removal by occupying powers. Repatriate Rashid frames its case around Egyptian stewardship and the significance of Rashid itself. The British Museum recounts the transfer under the terms of the military surrender and displays the original in London. The debate concerns who should decide where an Egyptian cultural object is kept and displayed.
